# Appendix C: Known Limitations {#sec-appendix-c .unnumbered}

This book's one non-negotiable rule is that a stated result comes from
a real run of this book's own code, not an estimate. The same standard
applies to limitations: everything below is something you can see for
yourself by reading the referenced script or rerunning the referenced
chapter, not a hypothetical concern.

Four of these are already called out where they happen — in Chapter
2's, Chapter 4's, Chapter 6's, Chapter 7's, Chapter 8's, and Chapter
10's own Production Reality or Field Notes sections — because that's
where a reader hits them first. They're repeated here, gathered with
two that aren't discussed elsewhere in the book, so you have one place
to check before pointing this pipeline at your own archive.

None of these are treated as bugs to quietly fix and forget. There is
no single report format across operators, contractors, and basins, so
no fixed set of extraction patterns, thresholds, or one small model
could honestly claim to be a finished, one-size-fits-all solution. This
book's actual goal is to give you the working knowledge to build and
adapt your own pipeline — this list is the specific starting point for
that adaptation work, not a warning to wait for a future version that
removes it.

## C.1 Report parsing breaks on a new report layout (Chapters 2, 6, and 7)

Chapter 2's and Chapter 7's extraction scripts both work the same way
a spreadsheet macro that looks for a value two cells to the right of
the label "WELL NAME:" works: reliable as long as every report is laid
out exactly the same way, and silently wrong or empty the moment it
isn't. Chapter 6's data-quality gate doesn't add a new regex of its
own, but it imports and runs Chapter 2's `extract_fields`/`extract_text`
unchanged, so this same fixed-layout assumption is what it's actually
checking against the whole 76-report archive.

`code/chapter_02/build_training_examples.py` looks for labels like
`WELL NAME:`, `PRESENT OPERATIONS:`, and `ACTIVITY PLANNED:` at fixed
positions in the report text using Python's `re.compile(r"...")`
pattern-matching syntax — its own docstring says so directly: *"Only
handles the 'DAILY DRILLING REPORT' field layout."* A completion
report, which uses different field labels entirely, isn't handled by
the main chapter at all — it's left to the challenge exercise.
`code/chapter_07/format_training_chunks.py` has the same shape: its
timeline extraction looks for a literal `TIME BREAKDOWN` header and a
fixed column order. Both chapters' own Production Reality sections
already say this plainly: Chapter 2's calls it "a specific, fixed field
layout — the one every `Drilling_NNN` report in this archive happens to
share," and Chapter 7's calls it "the same kind of assumption that
breaks the moment a different operator's report template shows up."

Chapter 6 puts a real number on how well that assumption held, at full
archive scale, on this one archive: `75/76` reports extracted cleanly,
with the single failure being the same completion-report layout
mismatch Chapter 2 already knew about. Chapter 6's own Production
Reality section is explicit that this number is a property of this
specific archive, not a guarantee: *"This archive comes from a single
well, a single operator's report template, over a few months. A
multi-well, multi-operator archive would show a much lower pass rate
here... A production quality gate would need a library of layout
patterns, not one regex per field."*

::: {.callout-important title="This is where a coding background starts to matter"}
This book is written for a reader with no prior programming
experience, and every chapter up to this adaptation step is written to
hold that promise. This step doesn't. Editing a `re.compile(r"...")`
pattern to match a different `TIME BREAKDOWN` or `OPERATIONS` table
layout — figuring out which characters in the pattern are literal text
and which are wildcards, then testing it against real report text until
it matches correctly — is a genuine programming task, not a
find-and-replace. If your company's daily drilling reports format these
sections differently from Utah FORGE's, expect this to be the point
where you need either to build real comfort with Python's `re` module
first, or bring in someone who already has it, before Chapter 2's or
Chapter 7's scripts will extract anything useful from your own
archive.
:::

**What this means for you:** if your own archive spans multiple
operators, contractors, or hand-written morning reports — each with
its own layout — expect to write a new set of label patterns per
format before Chapter 2's, Chapter 6's, or Chapter 7's scripts will
extract anything useful. None of the three attempts to detect or adapt
to a layout it wasn't written for.

## C.2 The faithfulness check compares words, not meaning (Chapter 10)

Chapter 10's `faithfulness_score` checks whether an answer's words show
up somewhere in the source text it's supposed to be grounded in — like
a word search, not a careful read of the sentence. It counts matching
vocabulary; it has no notion of which word is doing the work in a
sentence, so two short, common, opposite words can both "match" equally
well.

Chapter 10's own Field Notes catch this in a real run: report `#49`'s
grounded answer read *"Trip out of hole with fishing bha"* and scored
`0.80` faithfulness — well above the chapter's `0.5` threshold — against
a source that actually says *"Pick up Fishing BHA # 33 and trip in hole
to 7,996'"*. The direction is reversed and the specific depth is
dropped, and the score doesn't notice, because `"trip"`, `"fishing"`,
and `"bha"` all matched; only `"in"` versus `"out"` — the one word that
actually changes the meaning — flipped.

**What this means for you:** a high faithfulness score tells you an
answer's vocabulary came from the right report. It does not tell you
the answer's claims are correct. Any check built on this method will
have the same blind spot for a reversed direction, a flipped
up/down or in/out call, or a swapped number, whenever the rest of the
sentence's wording stays similar — exactly the class of error most
likely to matter on a real well.

::: {.callout-important title="An educational baseline, not a safety check"}
This is the limitation most worth taking seriously if you're
considering this pipeline for anything beyond learning. `faithfulness_score`
is a teaching tool for understanding what "grounded" does and doesn't
guarantee — it has not been validated as a safety system, and field
engineers who lean on automated summaries for safety-critical shift
handovers should never treat a passing score here as a substitute for
a qualified person reading the actual source. Report `#49`'s reversed
"trip in/out of hole" case above scored `0.80`, well past this
chapter's own `0.5` threshold — proof this check can pass exactly the
kind of error that matters most on a live well.
:::

## C.3 CPU training times don't demonstrate production scale (Chapters 8 and 13)

Every training run in this book is deliberately sized to finish on a
standard laptop with no dedicated GPU: Chapter 8's full multi-epoch run
over 669 examples takes about 30-35 minutes on CPU, and Chapter 13's
small continuous update — 2 epochs over 179 new examples — takes about
20-25 minutes on CPU. Both are demo-scale by design, not a benchmark of
what a production archive would take.

**What this means for you:** this book never measures, and doesn't
claim to know, how long a multi-epoch run over a full company archive
of thousands of reports would take on CPU alone, or how often a
Chapter-13-style continuous update could realistically run against new
reports on a standard corporate laptop. A dedicated GPU — mentioned in
Chapter 5 as an optional speedup (`model.to("cuda")`), never
benchmarked anywhere in this book — is the likely answer at real scale,
but that combination isn't something this book's own code has actually
run and measured.

## C.4 Resuming a checkpoint forgets the optimizer's memory (Chapters 8 and 13)

Training uses an optimizer (Adam) that keeps a running memory of how
each weight has been moving recently — similar to a mechanic
remembering roughly how much force a bolt needed last time, so the next
turn on it is smoother than starting from scratch. Chapter 8's
`save_checkpoint`/`load_checkpoint` functions save and reload the
model's trained weights, but not that running memory — it exists only
in the computer's memory while training runs, and is gone the moment
training stops, whether that's a real crash or a deliberate pause. The
chapter's own Production Reality section says so directly: *"this
simple version doesn't persist Adam's momentum across a resume, only
the model weights."*

Chapter 13's continuous fine-tuning reuses these same two functions
unchanged, so every scheduled update carries the same gap.

**What this means for you:** expect a small amount of extra training
noise — a temporary bump right after training resumes, before it
settles back into a smooth improvement — every time a paused or crashed
run is picked back up, and every time Chapter 13's continuous update
runs against a fresh checkpoint. It's a real, measured cost of this
version's simplicity, not a bug; a production setup would checkpoint
and restore that optimizer memory too.

## C.5 Everything in this book is tested on one small model (Chapters 1-13)

Every chapter from Chapter 1 onward loads the same base model,
`Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct`, chosen specifically because it fine-tunes on
CPU in the timeframes above — a deliberate choice matched to the
hardware check in Part 0, not a claim that it's the best model for
this job. `requirements.txt` installs `bitsandbytes`, the package
needed for QLoRA (fine-tuning a compressed, lower-memory copy of a
larger model — see Appendix B's glossary), but no chapter script in
this book actually loads a quantized model.

**What this means for you:** whether a larger model — 7B or 14B
parameters, fine-tuned with QLoRA instead of this book's plain LoRA —
would learn this same operational vocabulary better, more slowly, or
with different failure patterns on the same report archive is a real,
open question this book doesn't answer. If your own use case can afford
the extra memory and slower iteration a bigger model requires, that
comparison is worth running yourself; this book's code is not set up to
run it for you.

## C.6 The tokenizer's fixed vocabulary splits oilfield shorthand apart (Chapter 4)

A model doesn't read whole words — it breaks text into pieces from a
fixed list decided when the base model was built, the same way a
pre-printed form only has boxes for words someone anticipated. Chapter
4 shows this splitting `'BHA'` into two meaningless pieces, `['B',
'HA']`, with no more connection to "bottom hole assembly" than those
two letters carry on their own — a real result from that chapter's own
tokenizer script.

Chapter 4's own Production Reality section already names the fix this
book doesn't take: *"a production system dealing with truly nonstandard
shorthand... sometimes trains or extends a custom tokenizer instead of
just fine-tuning on top of a generic one; that's a heavier, rarer move
this book doesn't cover."* Chapter 5's fine-tuning never touches the
tokenizer itself, only the model's weights, so this split is present in
every chapter that follows.

**What this means for you:** the fine-tuned model in this book still
reads your operator's shorthand as arbitrary letter fragments, not as
a term it has a dedicated slot for — Chapter 4's own embedding check
shows it can still learn a useful association between `'BHA'` and
"bottom hole assembly" without a dedicated token, but that's a
different, weaker fix than giving the term its own vocabulary entry. If
your archive leans on internal codes or shorthand severe enough that
this isn't good enough, adding new tokens and resizing the model's
embedding table to match is the heavier step this book doesn't walk
through.
